title: Resilient, self-restoring power networks

concept.text: Concept synthesis: A resilient, self-restoring power network would coordinate protective equipment, power electronics, local generation, storage, and controls to recover electricity service after disturbances. It would isolate damaged or unsafe sections, divide surviving sections into independently supplied islands where feasible, stabilize those islands, and reconnect them safely when conditions permit. The intended advance is dependable coordination across a network, including equipment from different suppliers and situations in which communications are degraded or unavailable.

Technical synthesis: Grid-forming inverters would help local electrical resources establish voltage and frequency, while protection and switching equipment would disconnect faults and change network connections. Restoration controls would coordinate these actions with available generation, stored energy, and load. A locally sensible action must also preserve safety and stability elsewhere: energizing another section, changing a protection setting, or reconnecting an island can alter conditions throughout the connected system.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis: Dependable autonomous partitioning, stabilization, and restoration could substantially shorten outages where usable local resources and operable equipment survive. The revolutionary capability would be coordinated recovery across diverse networks under difficult conditions, reducing the delay between a disturbance and the safe return of service. The supplied material does not establish a numerical reduction in restoration time or a demonstrated reliability benefit.

Conditional downstream synthesis: If sufficiently affordable and broadly deployable, this capability could change how distribution networks and microgrids are designed and operated, and could support more reliable electricity access in difficult settings. Those outcomes additionally depend on resource availability, installation costs, deployment capacity, and maintenance. Automatic restoration cannot create missing energy, replace destroyed equipment, or eliminate the need for physical repairs; networks would still require adequate generation, storage, intact electrical paths, and operating reserves.

missing_breakthrough.text: Research-target synthesis: The missing capability is reliable coordination of protection, grid-forming power electronics, distributed generation, storage, and restoration controls across heterogeneous equipment under uncertain faults and communication failures. Individual components or successful local demonstrations would address only parts of this target. The broader challenge is ensuring that their combined behavior remains safe and stable as network connections, available resources, and loads change during recovery.

Engineering-barrier synthesis: A complete system would need to distinguish faulted sections from sections safe to energize, coordinate protective devices across changing configurations, establish stable islands with limited resources, sequence load pickup, and synchronize reconnection. When communications fail, local controls would need enough autonomy to sustain safe operation without allowing incompatible actions elsewhere. Interoperability, distributed decision-making, cybersecurity, and reliability engineering therefore intersect with the central electrical-engineering problem.

Scope qualification: These barriers define a coherent research target, but the supplied review could not verify documentary support for their full combination. Its source index contains no retained document text or artifacts. That limitation leaves the technical evidence incomplete; it neither rejects the concept nor establishes that no existing system has addressed any particular barrier.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a July 2022 NREL conference preprint attributed to Abhishek Banerjee and colleagues, titled Autonomous Microgrid Restoration Using Grid-Forming Inverters and Smart Circuit Breakers. It reports that the work proposed and evaluated autonomous restoration using those components, including simulations of black start—energizing a de-energized network—and network reconfiguration. The research points to the abstract and Figure 6, but the supplied review could not inspect either location or confirm the paper’s identity and contents. These are therefore attributed research reports, not independently verified demonstrations in this record.

The access limitation is specific: the source entry is marked not captured and has an empty artifacts array, with no saved passages, retained-copy completeness check, artifact hash, or verified locator available to the review. The supplied materials also refer generally to grid-forming inverter tests as pieces of the capability, but provide no inspectable test results or experimental scope. Missing extraction evidence is not evidence that the reported work is false.

Assessment synthesis: Even if the reported simulations are confirmed, simulated microgrid restoration would establish a narrower result than sustained, interoperable restoration across multiple real networks. It would not establish recovery from arbitrary faults or immunity to every combination of failures. The supplied freshness record is empty, so this material cannot establish subsequent progress or whether the full capability remains unresolved in November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Show interoperable operation across multiple real distribution networks with meaningfully different equipment, layouts, resource mixes, and operating conditions. Demonstrations should include planned islanding, representative equipment failures, communication loss, local stabilization, restoration of disconnected service where feasible, and safe reconnection. Specify the network diversity and failure coverage in advance so readers can distinguish demonstrated breadth from untested conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Interoperable recovery across multiple diverse real distribution networks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: Independently measure safety, restoration time, reliability, and cost against well-operated alternatives over sustained operation. Define operating duration, safety thresholds, comparator selection, and measurement independence before testing. Repeated trials and replication on additional networks should establish that success does not depend on a single installation or specially tuned equipment combination. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent sustained comparisons measure recovery performance, safety, and cost

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: Document the generation and storage required, the loads that can be restored, the physical damage that prevents recovery, the communication conditions tolerated, and the circumstances requiring human intervention or repair. Convincing success would mean reproducible recovery within a declared operating envelope. Finite tests can demonstrate broad coverage, but cannot establish literal universality, perfect stability, or freedom from blackouts under every possible combination of faults.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible recovery within documented resource requirements and operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ELE-05, Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply, could provide energy during prolonged shortages. ELE-09 concerns how available resources, protection, and controls maintain or restore service. Long-duration storage could make some islands viable for longer, but stored energy alone does not coordinate fault isolation or reconnection; restoration controls likewise cannot substitute for an adequate energy supply. The two entries remain distinct and complementary.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-10, Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing, could potentially supply distributed observations useful for fault detection and restoration decisions, if its measurements and communications meet network requirements. ELE-01, Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors, and ELE-07, Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery, concern different ways of carrying or delivering electricity. Such technologies could change network equipment and constraints, but would still require appropriate protection and control; none by itself establishes self-restoring network operation.

Scope synthesis: ELE-09 also overlaps with communications, distributed computing, cybersecurity, and reliability engineering because restoration decisions must remain coordinated under incomplete information and failures. This does not merge it with the roster’s separate computing, quantum-networking, neural-interface, switching, or photonic-computing innovations. Its defining outcome is safe recovery of electrical service, rather than a breakthrough in those underlying technologies.

unresolved_issues: The identity, July 2022 conference-preprint metadata, and reported contents of the linked paper remain unconfirmed by inspectable material in the supplied review.
The reported autonomous-restoration evaluation and black-start/reconfiguration simulations require retained source text or artifacts to verify their methods, assumptions, and scope.
The general reference to grid-forming inverter tests lacks specific experimental evidence in the supplied inputs.
No supplied freshness evidence establishes developments after the cited work or the field’s state in November 2026.
A future operational specification must choose concrete network diversity, failure scenarios, duration, safety thresholds, cost accounting, comparators, and independent measurement arrangements.
The magnitude of outage reduction, deployment cost, and effect on electricity access remains unquantified.

brief.title: Power networks that restore electricity themselves
possible: After a disruption, your electricity could return automatically as the network disconnects damaged sections, powers surviving areas independently and reconnects them safely. Equipment from different suppliers would coordinate recovery even when communications fail.
why: Coordinated recovery could shorten outages and reduce the wait for electricity to return safely. It could also help utilities provide more reliable service in places where electricity access is difficult.

sources.showed: A conference preprint describes simulations of automatic restoration in a small power network using electronic power controls and smart circuit breakers.
sources.cited_for: It supports simulation research on restarting and rearranging a small power network.
sources.not_established: Simulations do not establish dependable recovery across diverse real networks.

sources.who: University of Central Florida and Orlando Utilities Commission
sources.showed: A field test restarted a small, independently powered network using solar power and an inverter, a device that controls electrical output. It also tested electric vehicle chargers, whose reactive power demand used capacity without supplying useful energy.
sources.quote:
It is also observed that the level-2
charger draws a significant amount of reactive power which
is unbalanced in nature.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates restarting and balancing a real local network with solar generation and vehicle chargers.
sources.not_established: A local field test does not establish coordinated recovery across diverse networks or during communication failures.

sources.showed: Simulations and field tests combined fault isolation, independent operation and reconnection. The authors report that recovery time fell by over 50% compared with conventional strategies that disconnect demand to preserve stability.
sources.quote: A rapid self-healing architecture covering fault isolation, island detection, island stability control, and grid reconnection is established.
sources.cited_for: It supports coordinated recovery in regional networks and comparisons with conventional control.
sources.not_established: The reported tests do not establish sustained, independent comparisons across diverse networks and communication failures.

sources.who: E. Silva, M.E. Ropp and O. Lavrova
sources.showed: Simulations using manufacturers’ inverter models restarted a network, isolated faults and restored service using local measurements alone. Recovery depended on available power and intact electrical paths.
sources.quote: Black start, fault isolation, and system restoration are demonstrated.
sources.cited_for: It supports the possibility of automatic recovery without communication between devices.
sources.not_established: Simulation results do not establish reliable operation with physical equipment across diverse real networks.

shown: University of Central Florida and Orlando Utilities Commission researchers restarted a real local network and tested its interaction with solar generation and vehicle chargers. Chuan Zhou and colleagues report coordinated regional-network recovery in simulations and field tests, with less disconnected demand and faster restoration.

E. Silva and colleagues simulated recovery using local measurements alone. Together, these results demonstrate parts of the capability, but do not establish sustained recovery across diverse real networks with equipment from different suppliers and failed communications.
missing: Diverse real networks have yet to demonstrate dependable coordination through equipment failures, lost communications and safe reconnection.
Sustained independent comparisons have yet to establish safety, restoration speed, reliability and cost against well-operated alternatives.
Reproducible recovery needs clear limits for available energy, damaged equipment, demand and conditions requiring human repair.

milestones.label: Diverse real networks recover safely with different equipment
milestones.explanation: Multiple real networks would have to recover safely across different equipment, layouts, resources and failures, including lost communications. This would establish that coordinated recovery works beyond a specially arranged installation.

milestones.label: Independent sustained tests establish performance, safety and cost
milestones.explanation: Independent sustained comparisons would have to measure safety, recovery time, reliability and cost against well-operated alternatives, with repeated trials across networks. This would establish whether the benefits hold beyond isolated successes.

milestones.label: Recovery repeats within clear resource and operating limits
milestones.explanation: Recovery would have to repeat within stated limits for generation, storage, demand, damage, communications and human intervention. This would establish where automatic restoration can be relied upon.

uncertain: The size of the outage reduction, deployment cost and effect on electricity access remains unquantified.
The network diversity, failure coverage, test duration and safety thresholds needed to judge success remain open choices.

page.title: Autonomous restoration of AC distribution networks
page.definition: Alternating-current (AC) distribution networks automatically isolate faults, energise healthy sections as islands supplied by local resources, and synchronise them back to the grid. Protection, switches and grid-forming inverters, which establish voltage and frequency, coordinate across vendors through specified communication failures.

goal.need: U.S. electricity customers averaged 11 hours of interruptions in 2024, with major events accounting for 80% of interruption hours. EPRI’s utility-microgrid tests target autonomous resupply and reconnection without further customer interruptions.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Electricity
statements.quote: Autonomous self-healing protection schemes for a fractal grid
statements.context: The March 2026 draft microgrid control and protection strategy lists this among its research targets for interconnected microgrids.

statements.body: Universal Interoperability for Grid-Forming Inverters Consortium
statements.quote: The 20+MW demonstration Area is tasked to demonstrate the deployment of GFM technologies from multiple vendors that provide a range of grid services
statements.context: GFM means grid-forming. This passage describes the consortium’s demonstration work area.

completion.title: A multi-vendor distribution network restores and reconnects autonomously through communication failures.
completion.criterion: An operating AC distribution network with equipment from multiple vendors completes an operator-specified field test without restoration commands from a human. It isolates the specified fault, black-starts healthy de-energised sections, supplies the resulting islands and synchronises them back to the grid while designated operator–resource communication links are interrupted. Load service, voltage, frequency, protection and synchronisation remain within the operator’s specified limits, given the available generation, stored energy and intact electrical paths.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, combining the cited restoration, field-validation and communication requirements.
completion.basis: Searched DOE microgrid control and protection plans, IEEE 2030.8’s published scope, EPRI’s utility-controller protocol and UNIFI Version 3. These provide separate requirements for restoration, field validation and interrupted communications. No combined multi-vendor field acceptance test was found. The Atlas criterion combines those functions in one operating network.

milestones.title: Grid-forming inverters energise a dead network without an external voltage or frequency reference.
milestones.criterion: Resources designated for black start establish voltage without an external AC reference, supply transformer and load inrush within their equipment limits, and provide a voltage reference for other resources to synchronise. Banerjee and colleagues’ 2022 paper reports a laboratory demonstration with 12 inverters forming two microgrids initially loaded at approximately 30 W and 10 W.
milestones.set_by: UNIFI Consortium, Specifications for Grid-forming Inverter-based Resources, Version 3, section 3.2.2, for resources designated to provide black-start services.
milestones.threshold_quote: without an external voltage or frequency reference at the ac terminals.

milestones.title: A microgrid controller autonomously black-starts its island and passes EPRI’s eight functional checks.
milestones.criterion: After feeder blackout, the controller energises the full island and reaches steady state. All eight Table 10 checks pass, covering controller power, permissions, settings, isolation, resource modes, load-pickup sequence, status communication and system-condition checks. Skaria and colleagues’ 2024 field demonstration used a 2.5 kVA inverter to energise a 75 kVA transformer.
milestones.set_by: EPRI, Utility Microgrid Controller Test Plan, December 2023. The eight pass/fail criteria appear in Table 10.

milestones.title: An island reconnects autonomously with its online resources and supplied loads remaining energised.
milestones.criterion: With reconnection authorised and grid conditions stable for the configured service delay, the microgrid synchronises within site-specific tolerances and reconnects with resources online, loads energised and grid-connected settings restored. Zhou and colleagues’ paper, published on 3 June 2026, reports one field restoration example reaching reconnection in approximately 3.5 s after shedding approximately 2.9 MW.
milestones.set_by: EPRI, Utility Microgrid Controller Test Plan, December 2023, Synchronized Reconnection procedure and Table 12.
milestones.threshold_quote: the transition should not disrupt customers or cause unacceptable grid disturbances.

milestones.title: A fielded power system maintains specified operation when operator–inverter communications fail.
milestones.criterion: The power system and its grid-forming resources maintain the functions and operating limits specified by the system operator during delayed or interrupted operator–plant communications in field operation. Related simulations in Banerjee and colleagues’ 2022 paper joined three inverter-supplied islands through circuit breakers using local measurements.
milestones.set_by: UNIFI Consortium, Specifications for Grid-forming Inverter-based Resources, Version 3, section 3.4.1. The system operator specifies the required operation.
milestones.threshold_quote: function as specified by the system operator when communications are delayed or interrupted.

not_found: The NSF-hosted Silva, Ropp and Lavrova conference paper could not be opened after repeated attempts.
No opened study reports a complete pass of EPRI’s eight black-start checks or a field test of the cited UNIFI communication-interruption requirement.
No opened study demonstrates the complete restoration sequence in a multi-vendor operating distribution network with designated communications interrupted.

results.finding: One grid-forming inverter soft-started a 75 kVA transformer.
results.detail: The islanded demonstration also brought grid-following PV inverters online and supplied a charger. The text does not establish that transformer and load inrush stayed within equipment limits.
results.quote:
Fig. 2 demonstrates a soft blackstart of a 75
kV A transformer using a2.5 kV A GFM inverter.

results.finding: One field microgrid was black-started using a 2.5 kVA grid-forming inverter.
results.detail: The demonstration describes a black start and subsequent load supply, but does not establish an autonomous full-island restoration or report results for EPRI’s eight checks.
results.quote:
Fig. 2 demonstrates a soft blackstart of a 75
kV A transformer using a2.5 kV A GFM inverter.

results.finding: One simulated island reconnected approximately 3100 ms after the fault.
results.detail: The simulation describes resources supporting the island and reconnection, but does not establish the required service delay, synchronisation tolerances or restoration of grid-connected settings.
results.quote: At T4, GA line protection successfully recloses, and the regional distribution network reconnects to the main grid, resuming normal operation. The total duration from fault occurrence to reconnection is approximately 3100 ms.

results.finding: In one simulated black-start case, three grid-forming resources supplied an off-grid 13-bus system.
results.detail: The simulation starts with energised core microgrids; it does not establish that the inverters started without an external reference or supplied transformer and load inrush within equipment limits.
results.quote:
The black-start case is shown in Figure 3.  This figure shows the PSCAD model of the 13 -bus 
system, off-grid, with the three grid -forming IBRs.

results.finding: Three simulated microgrids self-assembled using local measurements only.
results.detail: The result is a simulation, not field operation during delayed or interrupted operator–plant communications.
results.quote:
This paper has demonstrated simulated self -assembly of three microgrids in the IEEE 13 -bus 
distribution test feeder, using exclusively techniques that rely on local measurements only .

results.finding: One Dalrymple grid-forming battery system black-started a network and picked up two 33 kV distribution feeders.
results.detail: Soft energization eliminated transformer and cable inrush, and the feeders were picked up at nominal voltage. The text does not establish that load inrush stayed within equipment limits or that other resources synchronized to the BESS voltage reference.
results.quote:
The ESCRI-SA Dalrymple BESS has demonstrated that the power supply can be quickly restored locally 
using an appropriate grid forming inverter with utility-scale energy storage.

results.finding: Santa Rita Jail microgrid: 1 whole-facility test achieved seamless islanding and resynchronization with the utility.
results.detail: The test reports resynchronization, but does not establish the service delay, reconnection tolerances, continued operation of all online resources and loads, or restoration of grid-connected settings.
results.quote:
At that point
all of the protective functions required by PG&E were success-
fully demonstrated and Santa Rita Jail was seamlessly islanded
and resynchronized with PG&E for the ﬁrst time.

results.finding: Dalrymple microgrid: 1 field event re-synchronised while supplying a 3.5 MW load.
results.detail: AEMO reports automatic line reclosing and battery-supported island operation. The report does not establish the configured service delay, synchronisation tolerances, or restoration of grid-connected settings.
results.quote:
The island was re-synchronised with the South Australia network at 622 s, 
corresponding to the actual time stamp of 15:03:09 hrs, when the Dalrymple – Ardrossan West 132 kV line 
was restored and began to supply the load (3.5 MW).

results.finding: One demonstration site’s microgrid system passed a communication failure test.
results.detail: The report says interconnection tests were conducted in the laboratory and after field installation, but does not specify the communication failure test conditions, the affected link, or the functions and operating limits maintained.
results.quote:
The following tests passed Rule 21 requirements, including: 
• Battery Charging Test 
• Battery Discharge Test 
• Communication Failure Test
